mockText: 100 items in 2 hours, with 4 drag-and-drop style items, flags and a review screen. Cisco doesn't publish the real item count, and on the real exam you can't go back to a question once you answer it. Practice the same way: answer each one and keep moving.
lead: Cisco's associate SOC analyst cert, called CyberOps Associate until February 2026. It proves you can monitor a network, read host and network evidence, and work an incident by the book. Same 200-201 exam, now version 1.2 with AI topics.

v12.label: v1.2
v12.note: One exam. Cisco renamed it from CBROPS to CCNACBR in February 2026; the content is v1.2, which added generative and predictive AI items. If you already held CyberOps Associate, Cisco moved you to CCNA Cybersecurity automatically.

domains.name: Security Concepts
obj: Describe the CIA triad
Confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Compare security deployments
Network, endpoint and app security; agent vs agentless; antivirus vs antimalware; SIEM, SOAR and log management; containers, VMs and cloud.
Describe security terms
Threat intel, threat hunting, malware analysis, threat actor, run book automation, reverse engineering, sliding-window anomaly detection, threat modeling, DevSecOps.
Compare risk, threat, vulnerability and exploit
How the four ideas relate.
Describe defense in depth
Layered controls so one failure isn't a breach.
Compare access control models
Discretionary, mandatory, non-discretionary, rule-, time-, role- and attribute-based; AAA.
Describe CVSS terms
Attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, scope, and temporal and environmental metrics.
Identify data visibility challenges
Gaps in network, host and cloud data that make detection hard.
Spot possible data loss in traffic profiles
Odd volumes, destinations and times.
Use the 5-tuple to isolate a compromised host
Source and destination IP and port, plus protocol, across grouped logs.
Compare rule-based and behavioral detection
Signatures vs statistical and behavioral baselines.

domains.name: Security Monitoring
obj: Compare attack surface and vulnerability
Everything reachable vs a specific weakness.
Identify data from monitoring tools
tcpdump, NetFlow, next-gen and stateful firewalls, application visibility and control, web and email filtering.
Describe what reduces visibility
ACLs, NAT/PAT, tunneling, TOR, encryption, P2P, encapsulation and load balancing.
Describe monitoring data types
Full packet capture, session, transaction, statistical, metadata and alert data.
Describe network attacks
Protocol-based, DoS, DDoS and man-in-the-middle.
Describe web application attacks
SQL injection, command injection and cross-site scripting.
Describe social engineering, including AI-generated lures
Manual and generative AI attacks.
Describe endpoint attacks
Buffer overflows, command and control, malware and ransomware.
Describe evasion and obfuscation
Tunneling, encryption and proxies.
Describe how certificates affect security
PKI, public and private keys, asymmetric vs symmetric.
Identify certificate parts in a scenario
Cipher suite, X.509, key exchange, protocol version, PKCS.

domains.name: Host-Based Analysis
obj: Describe endpoint security tools
HIDS, antimalware and host firewalls, using rules, signatures and predictive AI.
Identify operating system components
Windows and Linux: processes, services, file systems and logs.
Describe attribution in an investigation
Assets, threat actors, IOCs, IOAs and chain of custody.
Identify evidence types from logs
Best, corroborative and indirect evidence.
Interpret OS, SIEM, SOAR, app and command-line logs
Find the event in the noise.
Interpret malware sandbox reports
Detonation chamber and sandbox output.
Interpret artifacts
Hashes, URLs, and system, event and network data.

domains.name: Network Intrusion Analysis
obj: Map events to their source technology
IDS/IPS, firewall, application control, proxy logs, antivirus and NetFlow.
Compare impact and no impact
True and false positives and negatives, and benign events.
Compare deep packet inspection, packet filtering and stateful firewalls
What each one can see and decide.
Compare inline interrogation with taps
In the path and able to block, vs a copy for monitoring.
Compare tap data with NetFlow
Full packets vs transaction records.
Extract files from a TCP stream
With Wireshark and a PCAP.
Identify the key parts of an intrusion in a PCAP
Addresses, ports, protocols and payloads.
Interpret protocol header fields
Ethernet, IPv4, IPv6, TCP, UDP, ICMP, DNS, mail, HTTP, HTTPS, HTTP/2 and ARP.
Interpret artifacts to identify an alert
IPs, ports, processes, API calls, hashes and URIs.
Interpret basic regular expressions
Read and write simple patterns for log searches.

domains.name: Security Policies and Procedures
obj: Describe management concepts
Asset, configuration, mobile device, patch and vulnerability management.
Describe an incident response plan
The elements NIST SP 800-61 lists.
Apply the NIST SP 800-61 process to an event
Work a scenario step by step.
Map tasks to the NIST SP 800-61 phases
Preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident.
Map stakeholders to the NIST phases
Who does what, including CMMC.
Describe NIST SP 800-86 evidence concepts
Collection order, integrity, preservation and volatile data.
Identify network profiling elements
Throughput, session duration, ports used, critical address space.
Identify server profiling elements
Listening ports, logged-in and service accounts, processes, applications.
Identify protected data
PII, PSI, PHI and intellectual property.
Classify intrusions with security models
Cyber Kill Chain and the Diamond Model.
Relate SOC metrics to scope
Time to detect, contain, respond and control.

extras.title: Alert outcomes
rows: Alert fired, and the attack was real.
Alert fired, but nothing malicious happened. Tune it.
An attack happened and nothing fired. The worst one.
Real activity that's allowed or expected.

extras.title: The 5-tuple
rows: Usually a random high port on the client.

extras.title: Evidence types
rows: The original itself, like the actual log or drive.
Supports other evidence from a second source.
Circumstantial: you infer the fact from it.

extras.title: Order of volatility
rows: Network state: connections, ARP cache, routing table
Remote logs, monitoring data and backups

method: Use the five domains as your checklist. Security Monitoring is a quarter of the exam.
Learn the analyst workflow: alert, triage, investigate, classify, escalate, document.
Open real PCAPs in Wireshark, follow TCP streams and export files. Run Security Onion on your own lab machine.
Flashcards for protocol header fields, Windows and Linux logs, NIST phases and CVSS terms.
Full 120-minute practice exams. Cisco exams don't let you go back, so practice deciding and moving on.
tips: Cisco exams usually don't let you go back. Read every word, then commit.
Many questions show a packet or log and ask for one field. Know where the ports, flags and TTL sit.
When asked what comes next in an incident, answer in NIST SP 800-61 order.
There's no penalty for guessing, so always pick something.

quiz.q: A vulnerability can only be exploited if a user opens a crafted file. Which CVSS base metric captures that requirement?
o: User Interaction (UI:R)
Right. User Interaction is Required when a person has to do something, like open a file, for the exploit to work.
Attack Complexity
Complexity covers conditions outside the attacker's control, like a race condition, not a victim's action.
Privileges Required
That's about what access the attacker needs, not the victim.
Scope
Scope is whether the impact crosses into other components.

quiz.q: A system lets someone open payroll files only if they're in Finance, it's a weekday between 0700 and 1800, and their laptop is compliant. Which access control model is this?
o: Attribute-based access control (ABAC)
Right. The decision combines several attributes: department, time and device state.
Role-based access control (RBAC)
RBAC grants access by role alone. Time and device checks go beyond it.
Mandatory access control (MAC)
MAC uses classification labels and clearances set by the system.
Discretionary access control (DAC)
In DAC the file's owner decides who gets in.

quiz.q: Which monitoring data type lets an analyst rebuild the exact file a user downloaded?
o: Full packet capture
Right. Only full packet capture keeps the payload, so you can follow the stream and export the file.
NetFlow session data
NetFlow records who talked to whom, how much and when, but no payload.
Statistical data
Statistics show trends and baselines, not content.
Alert data
Alerts say a rule fired. They don't carry the whole file.

quiz.q: A web server log shows: GET /search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1-- HTTP/1.1. What attack is being tried?
o: SQL injection
Right. Decoded, it's ' OR 1=1--, which tries to make a database query always true.
Cross-site scripting
XSS injects script, like <script>, to run in other users' browsers.
Command injection
Command injection adds OS commands, like ; whoami.
Directory traversal
Traversal uses ../ to reach files outside the web root.

quiz.q: A finance clerk gets a call that sounds exactly like the CO, from an unknown number, urgently asking for a wire transfer before close of business. What is the BEST response?
o: Hang up and call the CO back on a number from the official directory to verify
Right. A cloned voice can be made with generative AI from a few public clips. Verify through a channel you already trust.
Send it, because the voice is clearly the CO's
A familiar voice is no longer proof of identity.
Ask the caller to confirm by email
The attacker controls the conversation and can send a spoofed or look-alike email.
Block the number and say nothing
Blocking stops this call, but the attempt should be reported so others are warned.

quiz.q: A firewall log shows the attacker's IP connected to a server at 02:10. The server's own audit log shows a new admin account created at 02:11. For the account creation, what kind of evidence is the firewall log?
o: Corroborative evidence
Right. It supports the audit log's record from a second, independent source.
Best evidence
Best evidence is the original record of the event itself, here the server's audit log.
Indirect evidence
Indirect evidence makes you infer a fact. The firewall log backs up a fact already recorded.
Hearsay
Logs from a system aren't someone's secondhand account.

quiz.q: A sandbox report for a suspicious file lists: creates C:\Users\Public\upd.exe, adds a registry Run key, queries x7k2-qz.top, then sends an HTTPS POST every 30 seconds. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
o: It sets up persistence and beacons to a command-and-control server
Right. A Run key survives reboots, and a POST on a steady timer to an odd domain is a beacon.
It's ransomware encrypting the disk
Nothing in the report shows mass file changes or a ransom note.
It's a normal software updater
Real updaters don't hide in C:\Users\Public and call random-looking domains every 30 seconds.
It's a worm spreading over SMB
There's no SMB traffic or scanning in the report.

quiz.q: On an Ubuntu server, where do you look FIRST for SSH login attempts?
o: /var/log/auth.log
Right. On Debian and Ubuntu, authentication events, including sshd logins, go to auth.log.
/etc/passwd
That lists accounts. It doesn't log logins.
/var/log/dmesg
dmesg holds kernel and hardware messages.
/proc/cpuinfo
That's CPU details, not a log.

quiz.q: A real SQL injection attack hit the web app. The IPS logged nothing, and you found the attack days later in the database logs. How do you classify the IPS result?
o: False negative
Right. An attack happened and the detection stayed silent. It's the most dangerous outcome.
False positive
A false positive is an alert with no real attack. Here there was no alert.
True negative
True negative means no alert and no attack.
True positive
That would need the IPS to have alerted on the attack.

quiz.q: Which setup can drop malicious traffic in real time?
o: An IPS deployed inline in the traffic path
Right. Inline devices see each packet before it moves on, so they can block it.
An IDS fed by a SPAN port
SPAN sends a copy. The IDS can alert, but the original packet is already delivered.
A network tap to a packet recorder
A tap also copies traffic. Great for evidence, but it can't block.
A NetFlow collector
NetFlow summarizes traffic after the fact.

quiz.q: You're responding to a compromised server that's still running. Following NIST SP 800-86, what do you collect FIRST?
o: The contents of memory (RAM)
Right. Collect the most volatile data first. RAM is lost on shutdown and holds processes, keys and network connections.
A full disk image
Disk data survives a reboot, so it comes after memory.
Logs on the central syslog server
They're off the box and stable. Grab them later.
Last night's backup
Backups are the least volatile of all.

quiz.q: Analysts record the attacker's phishing kit, a rented VPS used for hosting, and the HR office that was targeted, then link them with the threat group. Which model organizes an intrusion this way?
o: The Diamond Model
Right. Every event links adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim: the four points of the diamond.
The Cyber Kill Chain
The Kill Chain orders an attack into stages over time.
CVSS
CVSS scores vulnerabilities, not intrusions.
NIST SP 800-61
That's the incident response process, not an intrusion model.

pbqs.title: Map each event to its source
pbqs.scenario: Your SIEM pulled in six events. Pick the technology that produced each one. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
[1:2019401:3] ET WEB Possible SQL Injection Attempt [Priority: 1]
{TCP} 10.2.3.4:51022 -> 10.9.1.20:80
items.why: A signature ID, a rule name and a priority are what an IDS or IPS alert looks like.

items.log: %ASA-4-106023: Deny tcp src outside:198.51.100.9/51515 dst inside:10.9.1.20/3389 by access-group "OUTSIDE_IN"
items.why: A deny by an access-group on outside and inside interfaces is a firewall decision.
A URL, a cache result and a content type: this is a web proxy access log.

items.log:
Threat detected: Trojan:Win32/Agent
File: C:\Users\jdoe\Downloads\invoice.exe
Action: Quarantined
items.why: A named threat, a file path and a quarantine action come from antivirus on the endpoint.

items.log:
Src 10.2.3.45:52044  Dst 203.0.113.80:443  Proto 6
Packets 1,402  Bytes 1.9 MB  Duration 00:04:11
items.why: The 5-tuple plus packet and byte counts and a duration, with no payload, is a NetFlow record.

items.log:
Application: BitTorrent  Category: P2P  User: jdoe
Action: Block  Bytes: 0
items.why: Naming the application and its category, regardless of port, is application visibility and control.

pbqs.title: Classify the alerts and act
pbqs.scenario: Four items from this week's review. Classify each one and pick the next step. Each answer is used once.

rows.req: IDS alert “SQL injection” fired when a staff member searched the directory for the name O'Brien. The query was normal.
rows.why: The apostrophe in a real name tripped the signature. Nothing malicious happened, so tune the rule.

rows.req: An audit found a mailbox rule forwarding all of a user's mail outside for three weeks. No alert ever fired.
rows.why: A real compromise with no alert. Close the gap with a detection for new external forwarding rules.

rows.req: IDS flagged beacon traffic from FIN-07; EDR confirms an unknown process making the connections every 60 seconds.
rows.why: Two sources agree: it's real. Isolate the host and escalate with the evidence.

rows.req: No alerts overnight on the DMZ, and a log review shows only normal web traffic.
rows.why: No attack and no alert. Note the review and move on.
